the zebrafish displays anxiety-like behaviors such as dark- and wall-avoidance and habituates over time, that stress attenuates the expression of these behaviors and increases behavioral hyperactivity and that stress-induced patterns of behavior normalized over the course of a 5-min test.
zebrafish exhibit anxiety-like behaviors and coping strategies when exposed to a new environment and these behaviors are greatly impacted by prior stress history.
zebrafish exhibit anxiety-like behaviors and stress-induced changes to such behaviors in a novel environment.

understanding the behavioral repertoire of zebrafish in the context of a novel/unfamilar environment and how this repertoire is affected by a prior history of stress.
developing and validating behavioral paradigms that are relevant for stress research in zebrafishes.

developing translational models of stress and anxiety in zebrafishes, and our results suggest that zebrafish are suitable for studying stress-induced behavioral changes and the underlying neural and endocrine mechanisms.

the zebrafish is a useful model for the study of anxiety-like behaviors in the context of the light/dark-box and open field tests, and stress research.
the light/dark and open field tests are suitable for the study of behavioral responses to novel environment, anxiety-like behaviors, and stress in the zebrafish model system.
zebrafish are a suitable model for the study of anxiety and stress.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the light/dark and open field paradigms can be used to assess anxiety-like behaviors, exploratory behaviors, and behavioral hyperactivity in zebrafishes and that the effects of stress on these behavioral responses are similar to what has been reported in rodents.

zebrafish show similar behavioral responses in light/dark box or open field tests to that of rodents, which suggests that the zebrafish is an appropriate animal model to study the behavioral effects of stress and other environmental manipulations.
the behavioral repertoire of zebrafish is comparable to that of rodents.

zebrafish can be used to study the neurobehavioral consequences of acute and repeated stress in an ethologically relevant context.
the zebrafish model is highly useful for the study of behavioral responses to novel/unfamiliar environments and for the study of stress and coping in the context of environmental novelty.
